summary: This memo defines MIB objects for managing Frame Relay interfaces on data terminal equipment, using SMIv2. It is on the standards track at draft standard status.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the SNMP objects that describe a Frame Relay interface on a router or host: the link's management settings, each virtual circuit on it, and the errors the link has reported. A management system reads and writes these objects over SNMP.

how to monitor frame relay with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP objects a router or host uses to report on its Frame Relay link, its virtual circuits and their errors.

tldr.problem: A network manager needs to see what a Frame Relay interface is doing: which virtual circuits exist, what state they are in, how many frames each carries, and what errors the link has seen.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Management Information Base module, FRAME-RELAY-DTE-MIB, written in SMIv2, with three tables covering the Data Link Connection Management Interface, the circuits and the errors, plus one notification for circuit state changes.
tldr.outcome: The objects are reached through SNMP, and the values are grouped under the interface they belong to, which the RFC argues makes diagnostics simpler. The module obsoletes RFC 1315, of which it is a converted and extended version.

today: RFC 2115 is a Draft Standard published in September 1997. It obsoleted RFC 1315 and has not been obsoleted since. The module is the standard description of a Frame Relay interface for SNMP management, and it is written in the SMIv2 form that later MIB modules follow.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Framework and What This MIB Adds
sections.content:
The SNMPv2 network management framework has a few major components. RFC 1902 defines the Structure of Management Information, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. STD 17, RFC 1213, defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols. RFC 1905 defines the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The framework is adaptable and extensible by defining new MIBs to suit the requirements of specific applications, protocols or situations.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB. Objects in the MIB are defined using the subset of Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) defined in the SMI, and each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name. The object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object, and for human convenience a textual string, termed the descriptor, is often used to refer to the object type.

This memo defines a portion of the MIB for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets, in particular objects for managing Frame Relay interfaces on Data Terminal Equipments (DTEs). The module is named FRAME-RELAY-DTE-MIB and sits at { transmission 32 } in the MIB-II tree.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP managers read and write named objects, and a MIB is the catalogue of what those objects mean. This document adds the entries that describe a Frame Relay interface.

sections.title: Frame Relay as One Multi-Access Interface
sections.content:
For the purposes of this document, Frame Relay is viewed as a multi-access medium, not as a group of point-to-point connections. The model proposes that Frame Relay is a single interface to the network, the physical connection, with many destinations or neighbours, the virtual connections. This view lets a network manager group all the virtual connections with their physical connection, which allows simpler diagnostics and troubleshooting.

With the extension of the interfaces MIB it is possible to configure Frame Relay Data Link Connection Identifiers (DLCIs) as individual interfaces and create ifTable entries for each. The RFC says this is not recommended and is not directly supported by this MIB, and that in the presence of demand circuits it is not possible at all.

Where a user wants to group DLCIs together to associate them with a higher layer, or to associate a DLC with an unnumbered point-to-point service, the MIB provides two columns in the circuit table for it: frCircuitIfIndex, which is the interface the virtual circuit is layered onto, and frCircuitLogicalIfIndex, which points at the higher layer. The RFC's example runs a proprietary protocol over DLCIs 40, 41 and 42 and IP directly over DLCIs 20 and 30: the three DLCIs use the Frame Relay interface level for frCircuitIfIndex and the proprietary protocol for frCircuitLogicalIfIndex, while DLCIs 20 and 30 set both to the Frame Relay interface.

The RFC also lists how the standard interface objects are filled in for a Frame Relay interface. ifType takes the value allocated for Frame Relay interfaces, frameRelay (32). ifSpeed is the access rate for the Frame Relay interface, which can differ from the speed of the underlying physical interface: in a fractional T1 case the access rate could be 384 kbits/s while the underlying interface reports 1.544 Mbits/s. ifPhysAddress holds the primary address assigned by the Frame Relay interface provider, or a zero-length octet string if the interface has no address. ifInOctets and ifOutOctets count the information field, the user data, as well as the Frame Relay header and the CRC. ifInBroadcastPkts and ifOutBroadcastPkts are always zero, because there are no broadcast frames. ifHCInOctets and ifHCOutOctets are only required when ifSpeed is at least 155 Mbits/s, and ifHighSpeed returns 0 when the access rate is below 1 Mbits/s.
sections.plainLanguage: Frame Relay is one physical link carrying many virtual circuits, and the RFC asks managers to treat it that way, so that all the circuits on a link can be looked at together. Two columns in the circuit table say which interface each circuit sits on and which higher layer runs over it.

sections.title: The Data Link Connection Management Interface
sections.content:
The MIB is composed of three groups: one defining the Data Link Connection Management Interface (DLCMI), one describing the circuits, and a third describing errors. The DLCMI group holds the parameters that configure the link management itself, and it references the American National Standard T1.617-1991, Annex D.

Each row of frDlcmiTable describes one DLCMI and is indexed by frDlcmiIfIndex. The row carries frDlcmiState, which states which Data Link Connection Management scheme is active and by implication what DLCI it uses, with values noLmiConfigured, lmiRev1, ansiT1617D for ANSI T1.617 Annex D, ansiT1617B for Annex B, itut933A for CCITT Q.933 Annex A, and ansiT1617D1994 for ANSI T1.617a-1994 Annex D. frDlcmiAddress states which address format is in use: q921 with a 13 bit DLCI, q922March90 with an 11 bit DLCI, q922November90 with a 10 bit DLCI, or q922, the final standard. frDlcmiAddressLen gives the address length in octets, two, three or four, and for the Q.922 format the length covers the entire address including the control portion.

The rest of the row holds the timing and limit parameters: frDlcmiPollingInterval, frDlcmiFullEnquiryInterval, frDlcmiErrorThreshold, frDlcmiMonitoredEvents and frDlcmiMaxSupportedVCs, the largest number of virtual circuits supported, which is expressed with the DLCI type. The row also carries frDlcmiMulticast, frDlcmiStatus and frDlcmiRowStatus.

The DLCI type is one new textual convention introduced by this MIB. It refers to the range 0 to DLCINumber, where DLCINumber is by definition the largest possible DLCI value under the configured Q.922 address format. The MIB notes that interfaces may normally use 0 to 1023 but may be configured to use ranges as large as 0 to 2^23, and gives the type as Integer32(0..8388607). Introducing the textual convention has no effect on the syntax or the semantics of any managed object: objects defined in terms of it are always encoded by the rules that define the primitive type, so no change to the SMI or to SNMP is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The link management part of the MIB says which management scheme the interface uses, which DLCI numbering and address format apply, how often the link is polled, and how many errors are tolerated before the link is taken down.

sections.title: The Circuit Table
sections.content:
frCircuitTable holds a row for each Data Link Connection, or virtual circuit, attached to a Frame Relay interface, and each row is indexed by frCircuitIfIndex and frCircuitDlci. Discontinuities in the counters in this table are indicated by the value in frCircuitCreationTime.

frCircuitState says whether the virtual circuit is operational, with values invalid, active and inactive. In the absence of a DLCMI, rows may be created by setting the state to active, and deleted by changing it to invalid, although whether the row actually disappears is left to the implementation, so the object may read as invalid for an arbitrary length of time. Setting the state to inactive temporarily disables a circuit. The use of invalid is deprecated in this SNMP version 2 MIB in favour of frCircuitRowStatus, and the default value is active.

The row carries a set of counters and timestamps. frCircuitReceivedFECNs and frCircuitReceivedBECNs count the two kinds of congestion notification the link reports. frCircuitSentFrames, frCircuitSentOctets, frCircuitReceivedFrames and frCircuitReceivedOctets count traffic, and frCircuitDiscards counts frames discarded. frCircuitReceivedDEs and frCircuitSentDEs count discard eligibility messages. frCircuitCreationTime and frCircuitLastTimeChange are timestamps. frCircuitCommittedBurst, frCircuitExcessBurst and frCircuitThroughput carry the traffic shaping parameters. frCircuitMulticast and frCircuitType describe the kind of circuit, frCircuitLogicalIfIndex points at a higher layer running over the circuit, and frCircuitRowStatus manages the row.
sections.plainLanguage: One row per virtual circuit records whether it is up, how many frames and octets it has carried in each direction, the congestion signals it has seen, and the traffic shaping values configured for it.

sections.title: The Error Table
sections.content:
frErrTable describes errors seen on each Frame Relay interface, one row per interface, indexed by frErrIfIndex. Discontinuities in the counters in this table are the same as those that apply to the ifEntry associated with the interface.

frErrType records the type of the error last seen on the interface, with ten values: unknownError, receiveShort for a frame too short to demultiplex because the address field was incomplete or, for virtual circuits using Multiprotocol over Frame Relay, the protocol identifier was missing or incomplete, receiveLong for a frame exceeding the maximum length configured for the interface, illegalAddress for an address field that did not match the configured format, unknownAddress for a frame received on a virtual circuit that was not active or administratively disabled, and four values for problems with the link maintenance frames the DLCMI uses: dlcmiProtoErr, dlcmiUnknownIE, dlcmiSequenceErr and dlcmiUnknownRpt. The last value, noErrorSinceReset, means no errors have been detected since the last cold start or warm start.

frErrData is an octet string holding as much of the error packet as possible, with a size of 1 to 1600 octets. As a minimum it must contain the Q.922 address or as much as was delivered, and it is desirable to include all header and demultiplexing information. frErrTime is the value of sysUpTime when the error was detected. frErrFaults counts how many times the interface has gone down since it was initialised, and frErrFaultTime is the value of sysUpTime when the interface was taken down because of excessive errors, which is defined as the DLCMI exceeding the frDlcmiErrorThreshold number of errors within frDlcmiMonitoredEvents.
sections.plainLanguage: The error table records the last thing that went wrong on an interface, how many times the interface has dropped, and how much of the offending packet could be saved.

sections.title: Traps and Conformance
sections.content:
During normal operation, Frame Relay virtual circuits are added, deleted and change availability. Those changes matter to the network manager, so one trap is defined, intended as a corollary to the SNMP Link Up and Link Down traps: frDLCIStatusChange, whose OBJECTS clause is frCircuitState. It indicates that the indicated virtual circuit has changed state, meaning it has been created or invalidated, or has toggled between the active and inactive states. If the reason for the state change is that the DLCMI has gone down, per-DLCI traps should not be generated.

The trap is controlled by two objects. frTrapState says whether the system produces the frDLCIStatusChange trap, with values enabled and disabled and a default of disabled. frTrapMaxRate is the number of milliseconds that must elapse between trap emissions, in the range 0 to 3600000, with a default of 0, which means no minimum elapsed period is specified. If events occur more rapidly, the implementation may simply fail to trap, or may queue traps until an appropriate time.

The module also carries conformance information, with the object identifiers frConformance, frGroups and frCompliances under frameRelayDTE, and a compliance statement frCompliance whose mandatory groups are frPortGroup and frCircuitGroup, with frErrGroup and frTrapGroup treated differently.
sections.plainLanguage: One notification tells the manager that a virtual circuit came up or went down. It is off by default, and the manager can set a minimum gap between notifications so a flapping link does not flood it.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 1315
sections.content:
RFC 2115 lists the changes from the previously published version, RFC 1315. The module was converted from SMIv1 to SMIv2, which means that the table indices have access of read-only instead of not-accessible, the typical value for index objects in SMIv2. The module name was changed from RFC1315-MIB to FRAME-RELAY-DTE-MIB, and the textual convention 'Index' was dropped in favour of InterfaceIndex from the interfaces MIB module.

Two objects were added to the DLCMI table, frDlcmiStatus and frDlcmiRowStatus, and the enumerations for frDlcmiState gained two values, itut933A and ansiT1617D1994. The labels for the enumerated values of frDlcmiAddressLen were renamed to remove their hyphens, as SMIv2 requires, and it was clarified that the management virtual circuit, DLCI 0, is a member of the circuit table.

Seven objects were added to the circuit table: frCircuitMulticast, frCircuitType, frCircuitDiscards, frCircuitReceivedDEs, frCircuitSentDEs, frCircuitLogicalIfIndex and frCircuitRowStatus. The definition of frCircuitReceivedOctets was clarified as to which octets were counted. In the error table, frErrFaults and frErrFaultTime were added, the values of frErrType were clarified, and a size was added to the definition of frErrData along with an explanation of what data to capture. The object identifier for frameDelayDTE 4 was moved from frame-relay-globals to frameRelayTrapControl, and frTrapMaxRate was added. The RFC also created a set of object groups, a notification group and the compliance statements frCompliance and frCompliance0, and added ranges to frCircuitCommittedBurst, frCircuitExcessBurst and frCircuitThroughput.
sections.plainLanguage: This version is the earlier RFC 1315 rewritten in the newer management definition language, with more objects in the tables and clarifications about how the counters are counted.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues for this MIB are entirely covered by the SNMP Security Architecture, and have not been expanded within the contents of this MIB. The module defines no new security mechanisms of its own; the protection of the objects it defines is a matter for the SNMP framework in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security rules. Access to these objects is protected, or not, by the SNMP framework the deployment uses.

items.label: unknownError
items.desc: An error of a kind the MIB does not name.

items.label: receiveShort
items.desc: The frame was too short to demultiplex.

items.label: receiveLong
items.desc: The frame exceeded the maximum length configured for the interface.

items.label: illegalAddress
items.desc: The address field did not match the configured format.

items.label: unknownAddress
items.desc: A frame arrived on a virtual circuit that was not active.

items.label: dlcmiProtoErr
items.desc: An error occurred while interpreting a link maintenance frame.

items.label: dlcmiUnknownIE
items.desc: A link maintenance frame carried an invalid information element type.

items.label: dlcmiSequenceErr
items.desc: A link maintenance frame carried an unexpected sequence number.

items.label: dlcmiUnknownRpt
items.desc: A link maintenance frame carried an invalid report type.

items.label: noErrorSinceReset
items.desc: No errors have been detected since the last cold or warm start.

items.text: The access rate of the Frame Relay interface, which can differ from the speed of the physical interface underneath it.

items.title: Octet counters
items.text: ifInOctets and ifOutOctets count the user data, the Frame Relay header and the CRC.

items.title: Broadcast counters
items.text: ifInBroadcastPkts and ifOutBroadcastPkts are always zero, because there are no broadcast frames.

items.title: ifHCInOctets and ifHCOutOctets
items.text: Only required when ifSpeed is at least 155 Mbits/s.

items.title: ifHighSpeed
items.text: The access rate in Mbits/s, returning 0 when the rate is below 1 Mbits/s.
